sermon.title: Separate but Equal
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: Pastor David G. Kincer opens Titus 1:15–16 on defiled conscience, then tells how his father in 1951 taught him by action to reject “whites only” barriers. He recounts Brown v. Board as a unanimous moral overruling of separate but equal and calls Christians to treat all people right.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added from the speaker’s pauses and then corrected by hand, and obvious caption errors (names, Bible references) were fixed; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Editor notes: Personal childhood names (Willie/dad) kept in transcript; short answers avoid private living persons beyond historical public figures (Marshall, Warren, Eisenhower). Unverified 1956 49% survey. Historical details as spoken.

chunks.section_question: What does Titus 1:15 say about the pure and the defiled?
chunks.short_answer: To the pure all things are pure; to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure—even mind and conscience are defiled. People with good conscience try to act right; a seared conscience sees no reason to act naturally right—whatever you believe is right is right to you.
chunks.text: Titus 1:15. To the pure all things are pure to them there are defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure. See the people that have a good conscience and want to do right when they act they try to do everything with that consciousness of right. But when you have that conscience seared and hardened so much that you’re just doing evil then you don’t see any reason. To act in what is naturally right. Whatever you believe is right is right to you. But even their mind and their conscience is defiled and that’s what he’s telling he said you know their conscience whether they’re Christians or whether they’re non-Christians their conscience is what defiled it’s corrupt it’s evil it’s harmful they’re thinking their conscience is harmful.

chunks.short_answer: In 1951 as a child he saw “whites only” and “colored” fountains and thought disease; his dad drank from the colored fountain and had him drink—teaching by action how to treat people.
chunks.text: The one on the right said colored. Now I can read I’m I’m an eight nine year old kid do you know I can read and I and I go why why is there two fountains he said well that’s for the colored people and this is for the white people and in my little child mind this is honest this is honest to goodness truth I thought they must have a disease. And so the whites didn’t want to drink after them because they had some kind of d because I had been taught in school that disease was passed on by you know if you drink out of the same dipper we had to stop drinking on the same dipper down south we had to get our own glass and my so so mind goes they got a disease and I said well dad did they got a disease he got no disease I said well why can’t we drink out of that fountain he says we can’t he took me over there he reached down and drunk out of that fountain and then I drank out of the fountain my dad taught me by his action.

chunks.section_question: What did the “colored” balcony teach him?
chunks.short_answer: Dad took him to the balcony reserved for colored people—empty, graffiti, ripped seats, trash. Dad explained forced restriction of liberty makes people retaliate; the nine-year-old got it deep.
chunks.text: How to treat other people. Later that evening we went to the theater now in my local town there’s no balcony in the theater. And this theater there was a balcony and I was excited man I wanted to sit in the balcony that’s the place to sit man that’s that’s the chief’s seats. And I we walked by the stairs it went up to the back and said dad let’s set up in the balcony he goes no that’s for colored people I said well what do they have the best seats. How come they got the privilege of sitting in the balcony I said why can’t we sit there he said we can he took me by the handle we walked up to that balcony I got up to the balcony no one was there. But graffiti was all over the walls the seats have been ripped and torn there was trash everywhere where the theater people hadn’t even cleaned up.

chunks.section_question: How did Brown v. Board overrule “separate but equal”?
chunks.short_answer: 1951 NAACP suits (Topeka, Virginia, South Carolina) showed unequal funding ($30 vs $120) and harm from separation. Marshall argued; Davis never lost at SCOTUS. After Chief Justice died, Eisenhower appointed Warren, who framed it as a moral decision; unanimous overruling of 1896 separate-but-equal, implement quickly.
chunks.text:
My dad didn’t have to sit down and lecture me he showed me by his actions now it just so happens in that same year 1951 the NAACP. Had filed a lawsuit in Topeka Kansas Virginia. And a town in south Carolina. And in the south Carolina suit they were they were trying to show that separate but equal was not equal because the public schools gave. Like 30 dollars a month to the black schools and they gave 120 a month to the white schools and they were trying to show this is not equal but they put another little statement in there that said black children.

Are being harmed by the separation. In the public schools. And because they put that clause in there the judge said this has got to go to a higher court so they went to a higher court and they lost. Then they took it to the supreme court. And folks this is a it’s a tremendous story. The attorney for the NAACP was called Marshall. Who later became a chief justice of the supreme court. And uh. 1952. The supreme court heard the case. And then they were deliberating on it. Ike Eisenhower was voted into presidency that year they were still delivering on it in 1953 but the chief justice and the supreme court had a heart attack and died.

So Eisenhower appointed the governor of california. Who had never been in the judicial system at all as the new justice of the supreme court and the chief justice. Now these supreme court people were arguing and saying it’s all and their attorney Davis who never lost a case in the supreme court. Now Marshall was a black lawyer and Davis was a wildlife and Davis had never lost the case in the supreme court they called him the lawyer of lawyer. So they couldn’t get anywhere they were saying you know we got a the 14th amendment doesn’t. Allow this the law has been a law for 60 years now and the supreme court has upheld it as it’s not a law it was a ruling it wasn’t a law you got to get this in your head it was a ruling by the supreme court been that way for 60 years.

And they said we just can’t change it you know and and they were split and so they said you know we need another hearing and we want the attorneys to tell us what in the 14th amendment gives us the right to change this ruling and so they had another hearing in the meantime Warren. The governor of california. He started telling them this has got nothing to do with the 14th amendment. This has nothing to do because it’s been a ruling for 60 years. This is a moral. Decision. And he wrote a summary and presented it to them to make a long story short. The supreme court unanimously every one of them voted.

That yes not only is separation. Equal but separate not only the school. Was wrong for not having the same quality of education but equal but separate was wrong and folks he used the moral argument he won all the supreme court justices over and they unanimously voted and overruled the 1896 ruling of separate but equal they did say we got him to have time to figure out how to implement this and then they came back I think in 1954 or so and they said this has to be implemented implemented. Quickly right now.

chunks.section_question: Was America a moral nation yet still wrong on race?
chunks.short_answer: 1956 survey: only 49% believed Blacks and whites should integrate—yet SCOTUS won hope. Southern resistance: houses burned, killings, jobs lost. 1964 Civil Rights Act: vote, employment, public accommodations regardless of race. Dad as coal miner helped inbred hollow family at night; Christians should treat people right and show Bible truth.
chunks.text:
Now as you know the supreme court doesn’t make a law they make a ruling and so especially the whites down south. They are just up in errors about this in 1956 a survey that I found only 49 of Americans. Believed. That blacks and whites should be together. Mixed together integrated 49 and although 49 percent the minority of Americans believed it it won in the supreme court and I’m telling you that that we have when it doesn’t look like we have hope folks we got hope amen. Powerful well of course the southern states fought it I mean these people their houses were burned they they were killed they lost their jobs these people whether white or black paid a big price just like in the days when whites helped slaves be free they paid a big price they paid a price during that time.

Finally. And this went on for several years and I grew up in this. We were a moral nation but we were wrong. 1964 as you know they passed the civil rights act. Which stated that everyone can vote everyone can be employed everyone can go to a theater a restaurant of their choice any established place any public place. Regardless of the race their color or their national origin in other words if you’re born I don’t even care if you’re a one of these inbred we had inbred people down south and I remember our dad answering the door in the middle of the night this.

People that lived up in the hollow were inbred their features were distorted their children it it was horrible I mean you looked at them and oh it was it was good it was gross even as a child they were totally different and their son was sick and dying and my dad got up in the middle of the night who was a coal miner and worked hard and took this guy’s child down to the doctor and the boy died he found he did die and my parents went to that funeral what I’m telling you is I had parents that showed me how to treat other people because they treated other people right. Could that be an amen. And Christians in America should be treating other people right. And showing the Bible. Truth.

faqs.question: What year was the drinking-fountain story?
faqs.answer: 1951, when he was about eight or nine.

faqs.question: Did his dad drink from the colored fountain?
faqs.answer: Yes—and then had his son drink, teaching by action.

faqs.question: Why did Dad say the balcony was trashed?
faqs.answer: If someone forced and restricted your liberty, you would retaliate too.

faqs.question: What was his dad’s name in the story?
faqs.answer: Willie—an old man called him Willie about who rides in the car.

faqs.question: Who was the NAACP attorney?
faqs.answer: Marshall, who later became a Supreme Court justice.

faqs.question: Whom did Eisenhower appoint Chief Justice?
faqs.answer: The governor of California (Warren), who had never been in the judicial system.

faqs.question: Was “separate but equal” a law or a ruling?
faqs.answer: He stresses it was a Supreme Court ruling for about 60 years, not a law.

faqs.question: What argument won all the justices?
faqs.answer: Warren’s moral decision argument—not merely 14th Amendment technicalities.

faqs.question: What percent favored integration in the 1956 survey he cites?
What did the 1964 Civil Rights Act state?
faqs.answer: Everyone can vote, be employed, and use theaters/restaurants/public places regardless of race, color or national origin.
